title: Quantum transport in a non-Hermitian 1D synthetic lattice: from quantum Zeno reflection to near-perfect absorption
authors: Emmanuel. D. Mercado-Gutiérrez, W. Xu, E. Gvozdiovas, A. M. Piñeiro, Javier Argüello-Luengo, W. D. Phillips, Q. Zhou, I. B. Spielman
abstract: We experimentally explore the absorption of a propagating wavepacket impinging upon a dissipative region in an engineered quantum system. We employ a 1D non-Hermitian synthetic lattice with an abrupt interface between dissipative and non-dissipative subchains, using the states of the electronic ground-state hyperfine manifold in a $^{87}$Rb Bose-Einstein condensate as sites. By tuning the dissipation rate, we observe a progression from ballistic propagation, to near-perfect absorption, to quantum Zeno reflection. Guided by numerical simulations, we identify that optimal absorption occurs when tunneling and dissipation are properly matched, and find qualitative agreement with an idealized semi-infinite model across all dissipation regimes. Our results establish synthetic lattices as a versatile Quantum simulation platform for dissipation-engineered quantum transport and highlight controlled dissipation as a resource for tailoring quantum dynamics.
summary: The authors demonstrate the control of quantum transport by engineering dissipation in a synthetic lattice built from $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ BEC atoms. By tuning the loss rate relative to tunneling, they achieve near-perfect absorption at an optimum balance point, contrasting this with ballistic or Zeno reflection regimes. This establishes controlled dissipation as a powerful resource for tailoring quantum dynamics.
main_problem: The study experimentally explores wavepacket absorption when impinging on a dissipative region within an engineered quantum system, aiming to control quantum transport by tuning dissipation.
main_result: Optimal energy absorption is achieved by carefully matching the tunneling strength and the dissipation rate, demonstrating a controllable transition between ballistic propagation, near-perfect absorption, and Zeno reflection.
method: The research combines experimental measurements on an atomic BEC with numerical simulations using non-Hermitian tight-binding Hamiltonians to model wavepacket dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a 1D non-Hermitian synthetic lattice realized using the hyperfine manifold of a trapped $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ Bose-Einstein condensate. The lattice features an abrupt interface between dissipative and non-dissipative subchains.
key_observables: Absorption efficiency ($A$), occupation probabilities $P_j(t)$, and total probability $P_T(t)$.
important_parameters: Dissipation rate ($ ar{\gamma}$), inter-chain tunneling strength ($J_0$), and the ratio $ ar{\gamma}/ ar{J}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the system with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, comparing measurements against numerical simulations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate wavepacket occupation probabilities in three regimes (lossless, optimal absorption, Zeno reflection) and show parameter scans confirming that maximum absorption requires matching tunneling and dissipation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and Hamiltonian to presenting experimental observations across different dissipation regimes, followed by theoretical analysis using idealized semi-infinite models for confirmation.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controllable platform (BECs) to engineer open quantum systems, making it directly relevant to research in open quantum dynamics, engineered dissipation, and non-Hermitian physics.
